options.why: Plastic is made by people in factories.
Glass is made by people by heating sand.
Bricks are made by people by baking clay.

hints: Natural materials come from plants, animals or the ground.
Which one grows in nature?
Think about a tree. What material does it give us?
items.explanation: Wood is natural because it comes from trees. Plastic, glass and brick are made by people.

items.prompt: Natural or made by people? Sort the materials.
hints: Natural materials are found in nature.
Ask: did people have to make it in a factory or a kiln?
Start with wool. Where does it come from?
items.explanation: Wood, stone, wool and cotton come from nature. Plastic, glass and brick are made by people.

items.prompt: Match each material to what it is made from.
hints: Each made material starts as something natural.
Do the one you are sure about first.
Start with paper. Which natural material is it made from?
items.explanation: Glass is made by heating sand, paper is made from wood, bricks are baked clay and a woollen jumper is made from sheep's wool.

options.why: Paper soaks up water and goes soggy.
Cotton soaks up water.
A sponge soaks up lots of water.

hints: Waterproof means water cannot get through.
Which one stays dry on the other side when it rains?
Think about what a raincoat or a bucket is made of.
items.explanation: Plastic is waterproof. Water cannot get through it, so it is used for raincoats and buckets.

items.prompt: A material that does not let water through is ___.
hints: Think about what an umbrella must do in the rain.
The word starts with water.
It ends with a short word that means safe from.
items.explanation: A material that does not let water through is waterproof. Raincoats and umbrellas are made of waterproof materials.

items.prompt: Which material is best for an umbrella?

options.why: Paper would get soggy and tear in the rain.
Glass keeps water out, but it is heavy and can break.
Wool soaks up water.

hints: An umbrella must keep you dry.
It must also fold up and be light to carry.
Ask for each one: does it keep water out? Can it fold?
items.explanation: Waterproof fabric keeps the rain out, and it is light and bendy, so the umbrella can fold up.

items.prompt: Which one soaks up water best?

options.why: Plastic is waterproof. It does not soak up water.
Metal does not soak up water.
Glass does not soak up water.

hints: Soaking up water is called being absorbent.
Which one do you use to dry yourself after a bath?
Ask: which one would get heavy and wet if you dipped it in water?
items.explanation: A cotton towel soaks up water best. It is absorbent, so it is good for drying.

items.prompt: Choose all the materials you can see through.

options.why: Wood blocks light. We cannot see through it.
Metal blocks light. We cannot see through it.
Cardboard blocks light. We cannot see through it.

hints: See-through materials let light pass.
Think about windows and water bottles.
Start with clear glass. Can you see through a window?
items.explanation: Clear glass and clear plastic are see-through, so light passes through them. Wood, metal and cardboard block light.

items.prompt: Match each object to the property that makes it useful.
hints: Think about the job each object does.
What must a window let through?
Start with the raincoat. What must it keep out?
items.explanation: A window is see-through, a raincoat is waterproof, a towel soaks up water, a bridge is strong and a rubber band is stretchy.

items.prompt: Why are cooking pots made of metal?

options.why: Metal pots are hard and stiff.
We cannot see through metal.

options.text: Metal is strong and does not burn on the stove.

options.why: Metal does not soak up water. It is waterproof.

hints: Think about what happens to a pot on a hot stove.
Which property would a pot need near flames?
Ask: what would happen to a paper or plastic pot on the stove?
items.explanation: Metal is strong and does not burn or melt on a stove. Heat also passes through it easily to cook the food.

items.prompt: Nadia drips water on four fabrics. Which fabric is best for a raincoat?

figure.caption: Water test
head: Fabric
After 1 minute
figure.alt: Water test table. Fabric A soaked through. Fabric B a little wet underneath. Fabric C dry underneath. Fabric D soaked through.

options.why: Water soaked through Fabric A, so it is not waterproof.
Some water got through Fabric B.
Water soaked through Fabric D, so it is not waterproof.

hints: A raincoat must be waterproof.
Look for the fabric that stayed dry underneath.
Read each row of the table one at a time.
items.explanation: Fabric C stayed dry underneath, so no water got through. It is the most waterproof, which makes it best for a raincoat.

items.prompt: Which object will a magnet pick up?

options.why: Wood is not magnetic.
Plastic is not magnetic.
Glass is not magnetic.

hints: Magnets pull some metals.
Which object is made of metal?
Ask: which material is magnetic, iron or wood?
items.explanation: Iron is magnetic, so a magnet picks up an iron nail. Wood, plastic and glass are not magnetic.

items.prompt: Ravi says all metals are magnetic. Which result shows he is wrong?

options.text: A magnet picks up an iron nail.
options.why: This shows iron is magnetic. It does not test other metals.

options.text: A magnet does not pick up a wooden block.
options.why: Wood is not a metal, so this does not test his idea.

options.text: A magnet picks up a steel paperclip.
options.why: Steel is magnetic, so this fits his idea.

options.text: A magnet does not pick up an aluminium can.

hints: To show an idea is wrong, find one example that does not fit.
You need a metal that a magnet does not pick up.
Check each result. Is the object a metal? Did the magnet pick it up?
items.explanation: An aluminium can is metal, but a magnet does not pick it up. So not all metals are magnetic. Iron and steel are magnetic.

items.prompt: Why are bicycle tyres made of rubber?

options.text: Rubber is bendy and grips the road.

options.why: Most rubber is not see-through, and tyres do not need to be.
Rubber is waterproof.
A heavy tyre would make the bicycle hard to ride.

hints: Think about what a tyre must do on a bumpy road.
Squeeze a rubber ball in your mind. What happens?
Ask: which property helps a tyre not slip?
items.explanation: Rubber is bendy, so the tyre squashes over bumps. It also grips the road, so the bicycle does not slip.

items.prompt: Which two properties does a window need?

options.why: A soft, stretchy window would sag and tear.
A window must keep its shape and keep the rain out.
A window should keep rain out, so it must not soak up water.

hints: Think about two jobs a window does.
It lets light in. What must it keep out?
Check both words in each choice.
items.explanation: A window must be see-through to let light in and waterproof to keep rain out. Glass has both properties.

items.prompt: Design a raincoat for a puppy. Label the material you chose and say why.

criteria.label: Draws a raincoat that covers the puppy's back
Writes one reason for choosing it

hints: Think about which materials keep water out.
Remember the water test: which fabrics stayed dry?
items.explanation: A raincoat must be waterproof so the rain cannot get through. Plastic or waterproof fabric would keep the puppy dry.

items.prompt: Hiro pours 10 spoons of water onto each fabric. How many spoons did Fabric B stop?

head: Fabric
Spoons poured
Spoons that came through
figure.alt: Table: Fabric A, 10 spoons poured, 8 came through. Fabric B, 10 poured, 3 came through. Fabric C, 10 poured, 0 came through.

hints: Find the row for Fabric B.
Some water came through. The rest was stopped.
Start with 10 spoons and take away the ones that came through.
items.explanation: 10 spoons were poured on Fabric B and 3 came through. 10 take away 3 is 7, so Fabric B stopped 7 spoons.
